awd_titl_txt: Workshop on Future Plans for Geotechnical Extreme Events Reconnaissance (GEER); Reston, Virginia; Spring 2026
awd_abstract_narration:
The Geotechnical Extreme Events Reconnaissance (GEER) Association provides for investigation, data collection and public dissemination of information from natural disasters. GEER’s mission to “turn disasters into knowledge” benefits the geotechnical engineering profession by providing information that can improve design and construction practices to reduce poor performance in extreme events; benefits the engineering profession by fostering innovative methods to perform reconnaissance to learn from extreme events; and benefits society by improving the management of risk in future extreme events. This project intends to identify opportunities for improvement moving forward to ensure the objectives remain relevant and new and emerging technologies are leveraged.

The methodology will be to conduct a two-day workshop to discuss and brainstorm opportunities for GEER. Specific objectives include identifying priorities for future efforts, developing best practices for incorporating new technology, and reshaping governance to provide adaptability and transparency. The workshop will include invited talks by professionals (academics and practitioners) with GEER experience, as well as panels shaped around specific questions and objectives. It will involve 30  participants intended to provide representation from senior and junior levels, people who have led and/or participated in GEER activities for many years and people who have not, people with a broad range of perspectives about different types of extreme events, and people with knowledge about a variety of geographic regions. The workshop will be preceded by an online survey among GEER members to collect additional input on critical topics that should be addressed during the workshop. The product of the workshop will be a report summarizing the discussions and providing guidance for the future of GEER.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Geotechnical Extreme Events Reconnaissance Association provides for investigation, data collection and public dissemination of information from natural disasters. GEER’s mission to “turn disasters into knowledge” benefits the geotechnical engineering profession by providing information that can improve design and construction practices to reduce poor performance in extreme events; benefits the engineering profession by fostering innovative methods to perform reconnaissance to learn from extreme events; and benefits society by improving the management of risk in future extreme events. GEER has been sponsored by the National Science Foundation for more than 20 years. This project was intended to identify opportunities for improvement moving forward to ensure the objectives remain relevant and new and emerging technologies are leveraged.

The methodology was to conduct a two-day workshop to discuss and brainstorm how GEER could be improved. Specific objectives included identifying priorities for future efforts, developing best practices for incorporating new technology, and reshaping governance to provide adaptability and transparency. The workshop included invited talks by professionals (academics and practitioners) with GEER experience, as well as panels shaped around specific questions and objectives. It comprised 47 participants providing broad representation considering career stage, GEER experience, technical expertise and geographic familiarity. The workshop was preceded by an online survey among GEER members to collect additional input on topics to be addressed during the workshop. The product of the workshop was a report summarizing the discussions and providing guidance for the future of GEER.

The recommendation coming from the workshop was transition GEER into a self-sustaining, multi-hazard, full-life-cycle professional institution governed with transparency and interdisciplinary agility. The following guidelines were provided to help achieve this goal:

1. Broaden Hazard Scope & Define Deployment Thresholds

  • Beyond Earthquakes & Hurricanes: Formally expand GEER’s operational scope to encompass non-seismic, cascading, chronic, and anthropogenic hazards—including wildfires (hydrophobicity/debris flow), coastal scour, tailings/dam failures, permafrost thaw, karst sinkholes, and structural/facility collapses.
  • Deployment Thresholds: Trigger missions based on data perishability, regional anomaly, and transferable geotechnical learning potential rather than event magnitude alone.
  • Cascading Risk Frameworks: Include complex hazard chains (e.g., Wildfire  Landslide  River Damming  Flooding  Infrastructure Failure) to avoid compartmentalized assessments.

2. Modernize Field Technology & Data Curation

  • Emerging Technologies: Form a dedicated GEER Committee on Emerging Technologies to advance the integration of autonomous robotics, fiber-optic sensing, remote sensing, AI processing of large datasets, and rapid subsurface characterization tools (e.g., porewater and saturation profiling).
  • Data Transparency & Curation: Mandate the rapid upload of all geotagged field data to DesignSafe with assigned DOIs. Standardize training in field data acquisition to ensure data quality across multi-scale and pre- vs. post-event performance observations.

3. Reframe Reconnaissance as a Full Project Life Cycle

  • Pre-Event Phase: Establish a Pre-Event Data Committee and a pilot "Adopt-a-Region" initiative (enabling firms/universities to collect baseline LiDAR and geospatial data in exchange for equipment access) to build baseline datasets before events occur.
  • Operational Execution: Standardize field activation, daily track/photo logging, virtual-field team coordination, and tracking apps (e.g., SiteEye / Sahagozu).
  • Multi-Tiered Dissemination Policy: Update operational procedures to enforce a three-stage publishing pipeline:
    1. Immediate (Days): 1-page plain-language public summary / press release / video.
    2. Short-Term (Weeks): Early-release field summary report.
    3. Final (Months): Comprehensive GEER report complete with research seeds.
  • Clear Operational Endpoints: Restrict GEER’s direct role to capturing perishable data and framing research questions to avoid legal liabilities associated with long-term monitoring. Transition longitudinal studies to designated local leads.

4. Drive Practice and Policy Impact

  • Translational Pathways: Actively track long-term impacts on design standards, building codes, and policy (e.g., state legislation, OpEds, ASCE Public Policy Committee links).
  • Community Dissemination: Institutionalize regular GEER technical sessions at Geo-Congresses, coordinate with the NHERI Technology Transfer Committee, and build a culture of post-mission follow-up.

5. Modernize Governance & Ensure Financial Sustainability

  • Governance Transition: Shift from a single PI-centric model toward an independent 501(c)(3) non-profit entity (similar to USUCGER) governed by an elected Board of Directors, decentralized sub-committees (by hazard/region), an Ombud position, and a dedicated Executive Director.
  • Diversified Funding Model: Form an Endowment & Corporate Committee to secure corporate sponsorships and long-term endowment funds. Establish formal agency contracts (USGS, USACE, NOAA, NIST, FEMA) and offer monetized training workshops for industry while keeping individual and student membership free.
  • Year-Round Engagement: Host an Annual Hybrid GEER Meeting, institute early-career mentorship programs, and establish virtual "Home-Team" rosters (remote GIS, data curation, literature reviews) to keep the community continuously engaged between major disaster events.
